newsitem.title: FRANCE: What to expect from French public finances audit.
newsitem.headline: What to expect from French public finances audit.

text.p: An audit of public finances ordered by France's new Socialist-led government will be released on Monday (July 21). Following are details of the motives for holding the audit, who is conducting it and what to expect.
MOTIVES
The government says it wants details of the state of public finances before deciding measures to curb the public deficit.

It is following an example set by former prime minister Edouard Balladur, who ordered an audit after the centre-right regained power in 1993 to look at the state of public finances after five years of Socialist government.

The conservative opposition says the new audit is purely political, allowing the government to blame its predecessors for the public finances it is inheriting. It says the government already knows the details of public finances.
METHOD AND TIMING OF ANNOUNCEMENT
The audit is being carried out by two members of the Court of Auditors, Philippe Nasse and Jacques Bonnet.
Nasse and Bonnet will present the results of the audit to a closed-door hearing of the parliamentary finance committee at 0900 GMT on Monday.
Finance Minister Dominique Strauss-Kahn is to testify before the same committee at 1300 GMT.
The results of the audit will also be made public on Monday, although no time has yet been fixed.
WHAT TO EXPECT
1997 BUDGET
The audit will forecast the total public deficit, which comprises central government spending, welfare and local authority spending, for this year.

President Jacques Chirac has said the deficit is running at around 3.5 percent of gross domestic product, compared to 3.0 percent forecast in the 1997 Finance Act. Government sources have said it may be slightly above 3.5 percent.

The auditors are expected to give a revised figure for the central government budget deficit and welfare deficit forecast in the 1997 Finance Act at 284 billion francs ($46.9 billion) and 30 billion francs respectively.

To provide a complete picture of public finances, the auditors would also need to calculate the potential surplus or shortfall in national unemployment fund UNEDIC and in local authority budgets and other areas of state spending.
A leaked letter from former prime minister Alain Juppe to Prime Minister Lionel Jospin, dated June 2, gave the following details on the 1997 budget:

-- Total revenues are seen at around 35 billion francs less than expected, due to a 15 billion franc shortfall in central government revenues, mainly VAT (sales tax), a 10 billion franc shortfall in payroll taxes to finance welfare spending and the loss from budget of a nearly 12 billion franc surplus previously expected from national unemployment fund UNEDIC.

-- Total spending needs are seen at 23 billion francs more than expected, partially offset by five billion franc savings on debt service charges and a centre-right spending freeze on 10 billion francs in credit lines. Juppe said this would leave only eight billion francs to be covered.
The new government however has since partially reversed the 10 billion franc spending freeze.
1997 WELFARE DEFICIT

The central social security accounts, which use payroll taxes to fund pensions, healthcare and family benefits, are expected to show a deficit some five billion francs more than the 30 billion francs originally expected, while there is a deficit of a further five billion in other social security accounts, Juppe said.
The government could save some money on welfare this year through a plan to limit family allowances for the higher paid.
ACCUMULATED WELFARE DEFICIT
Juppe however warned the government it needed to take action to deal with the accumulated welfare deficit in 1996 and 1997.

The previous government set up last year a welfare debt repayment fund, CADES, which is borrowing on capital markets to fund the debt and using proceeds from a new tax, the RDS, to repay it. CADES however only covered debt up to the end of 1995, plus a forecast deficit of 17 billion in 1996.

Since the 1996 deficit turned out to be 55 billion francs, the government needs to take action to deal with the remaining 38 billion franc deficit uncovered in 1996, plus a deficit of 35 billion or so this year and possibly any new deficits expected next year. The welfare system is currently being financed by temporary advances from state bank Caisse des Depots et Consignations.
1997 BUDGET REDUCTION MEASURES
The government is expected to announce measures to reduce the deficit this year soon after the release of the audit.
Strauss-Kahn has said France will not cut the deficit as far as 3.0 percent of GDP this year, but will try to reduce the figure forecast in the audit by a few percentage points.
Newspapers have suggested the government may try to cut the deficit to around 3.3 percent of GDP.
Strauss-Kahn has declined to confirm this target, saying the government will aim for what it thinks the economy can tolerate.

He has said measures to reduce the deficit could affect companies and well-off households as well as involving savings on planned spending. Any increase in company taxes, if there were to be such a rise, would be designed in such a way as not to hamper business investment.
1998 BUDGET
The government may announce plans to curb the deficit further in 1998 to reduce it to three percent of GDP in order to allay European fears about the deficit overshoot this year.

Juppe in his letter warned that the trend in public deficits pointed to a figure above four percent of GDP next year but said this could be cut to three percent "after savings on budget and welfare spending, questioning some fiscal spending and tapping exceptional non-fiscal revenues."
Economic growth was not having a strong enough effect on government and welfare revenues to allow the deficit to fall spontaneously, Juppe said.
Strauss-Kahn has said that if the audit shows a deficit this year of 3.4 percent it will be easier to bring it into line next year than if it shows 3.8 percent this year.
-- Myra MacDonald Paris Newsroom +33 1 42 21 53 81 ($ = 6.050 French Francs)
